newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SA WEEK AHEAD-SAfrica ca deficit seen swelling Q1.
newsitem.headline: SA WEEK AHEAD-SAfrica ca deficit seen swelling Q1.

text.p: South Africa's current account deficit is expected to have swelled dramatically in the first quarter of 1997 after a high services bill offset the effects of a healthier trade surplus, economists said.

According to 10 economists in a Reuters' consensus poll, the current account gap will jump to an unadjusted 2.1 billion rand compared with a 50 million rand shortfall in the fourth quarter of 1996. Figures are due at 1500 GMT on Thursday in the Reserve Bank's latest quarterly bulletin.
The range of forecasts was for a deficit of between 500 million and three billion rand, with eight of the economists forecasting a shortfall of two to 2.5 billion rand.

The services account, which was expected to show a shortfall of around 4.5 billion rand for the quarter, was likely to be hit by weak tourism receipts and offshore payments on domestic bonds and shares, economists said.
"Tourism is not doing that well and that will come into our receipts of foreign funds for tourism," Mathison and Hollidge economist Henry Flint said.
Travel allowances for local residents, which were increased to 80,000 rand per individual, could have also had a negative impact on services.
"That should also start showing in the figures in terms of a larger net outflow of tourist spending, one of the major components of the services account," an economist said.
Economists said a further drain could have come from coupon and dividend payments to foreigners who were heavy buyers of local shares and gilts in the period.
Equisec economist Dawie Roodt noted, however, that some interest payments offshore could have been reinvested locally, trimming the deficit on the services account.
Another economist said freight costs might have helped lower the account gap. "The only thing that might have improved is freight costs given slightly lower imports," he said.
The trade balance was more difficult to predict, as the monthly data includes Botswana, Lesotho, Namibia and Swaziland.
Most felt, however, that a two billion rand trade surplus for the quarter was likely.

Economists said that despite the expected increase in the deficit in the first quarter, the current account for the year as a whole was expected to show an improvement on last year's 8.5 billion rand shortfall
Sanlam senior economist Pieter Calitz said he expected a stronger trade surplus to come to the current account's rescue as the year progresses.
"I expect that later in the year we will see better export figures and as the economy cools further...we will see lower imports," Calitz said.
Syfrets economist Sandra Gordon added that strengthening European economies and healthier commodity prices would also contribute to an improved current account deficit for the year.
